messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For most of his career, Minh Tran had been the one people called in crisis. At 68, a widowed public defender with a reputation for steadiness, he was used to walking into courthouse holding cells and hearing frightened, angry stories without losing his bearings. That changed after his adult daughter was killed during a home invasion six months ago. He was not there when it happened, but he arrived soon afterward, and what has stayed with him is not a coherent sequence so much as shattered fragments: the front door ajar, a lamp overturned, the sound of a neighbor crying in the hallway, and, most piercingly, a short burst of his daughter’s voice on the 911 recording that police later played for him. In his mind, the memories do not settle into a single account. They come in jagged pieces, and when they do he hears sounds as if they are happening again—the panic in her voice, the banging at the door, the operator asking questions no one could answer in time. Each return of the memory is soaked in overwhelming grief.

In the first weeks after the funeral, Minh tried to manage those intrusions in the practical way he approached everything else. He stopped watching the evening news and turned off legal dramas or crime shows as soon as a break-in or assault appeared. He began eating constantly in the late evenings, telling himself that a full stomach gave him something else to feel besides the hollow drop that came when his daughter’s voice intruded. The more the memory arrived in those broken sensory flashes, the more urgently he looked for ways to block it out. He could not bear anything on television or in the newspaper that resembled what had happened to her, because even a brief story about violence was enough to pull him back into those disconnected moments and the grief they carried.

Those same fragments also left him feeling as if danger were immediate and unfinished. Because he could not hold the event in his mind as something completed, he reacted to ordinary sounds as if they signaled another attack. A knock in his apartment building, footsteps outside his door, voices rising in the street at night could set off a surge of fear before he had even oriented himself. He became preoccupied with locks and windows, checking them repeatedly before bed and again after waking in the night, not because he thought through a specific threat each time but because his body seemed convinced that someone could force their way in at any moment. What frightened him most was how quickly he went from sitting in his armchair to standing breathless in the hallway, certain for a second that something was wrong.

That sense of danger spread into his work. At the courthouse, Minh found himself scanning faces in waiting areas and elevators, vigilant for men who seemed agitated, intoxicated, or unpredictable. He had spent decades around distressed defendants and distraught families, but now he watched people with a strained, suspicious attention that exhausted him. When a client raised his voice in an interview room, Minh felt the old jolt of alarm and afterward checked his office door twice before leaving. Because he felt perpetually on edge, he leaned harder on the habits that seemed to contain it: more checking, more avoidance of media, more eating after work to settle himself. For an hour or two these things dulled the fear, but they also kept his world organized around the possibility of danger, so that every unvetted sound or unfamiliar person seemed to require even more vigilance.

The cycle tightened over the following months. Nights were the worst. After checking the deadbolt, he would lie down, hear a creak in the building, and suddenly the broken pieces of the night of his daughter’s death would flare up again, especially the sounds. He would get back out of bed to inspect the windows, then stand in the kitchen eating cereal or leftover rice straight from the container, trying to push the audio fragments out of his head. By morning he was ashamed of how little control he had, yet the poor sleep and constant alertness made the memories easier to trigger again the next day. Even at work, after reading case files involving assault or burglary, he would avoid related coverage online and leave his office to make another round of checking the door, all while the same clipped sounds replayed internally.

Lately, Minh has started to worry that he is becoming someone his daughter would not recognize: a man who mistrusts strangers, startles at harmless noises, and spends his evenings circling his apartment to make sure it is secure. The change has begun to affect his work; he has shortened client meetings, avoided certain assignments when he can, and once snapped at an investigator who came up behind him unexpectedly in the office. He finally sought help after finding himself frozen at home one night, hand on the lock, hearing his daughter’s voice so vividly that he could not tell for a moment whether it was memory or something happening outside his own door. He says he is afraid that if this continues, he will never again feel that the world is anything but moments away from taking another person he loves, and he hopes, cautiously, that treatment might help him remember his daughter without being dragged back into the sound of losing her.
